pages.title: On-demand supplies

blocks.v: An _on-demand_ supply produces its values anew for every tap. `Supply.from-list` is on-demand: each tap gets the **whole** sequence from the start, independently of any other tap.

Both taps received all three values. The supply did not “use up” its values on the first tap; it simply ran again for the second. This is the behaviour you want when a supply represents a fixed source — a list, a file, a query — that every subscriber should see in full.

On-demand is the default for supplies built from existing data, because each consumer naturally expects the complete sequence. The other kind, a _live_ supply, behaves quite differently, as the next topic shows.

prompt.v: For an **on-demand** supply such as `Supply.from-list`, what does a second tap receive?

options.text: Nothing — the first tap used up the values
Only the values emitted after it tapped
The whole sequence, from the start

explanation.v: An on-demand supply replays its values for every tap. Each tap is independent and receives the complete sequence from the beginning — unlike a live supply, where late subscribers miss earlier values.

pages.title: Live supplies

blocks.v: A _live_ supply broadcasts values as they occur to whatever taps are listening **at that moment**. You create one with a `Supplier`: the supplier is the sending end, and its `.Supply` is the receiving end that others tap.
Here `.emit` pushes a value into the live supply, and every current tap receives it. The tap was in place before the emissions, so it captured both values.

The crucial difference from an on-demand supply is timing: a live supply does **not** remember past values. A tap added after an `emit` would miss whatever was emitted before it subscribed. Live supplies are the right model for real events — clicks, messages, sensor readings — where “what is happening now” matters and the past is gone.
In short: use an on-demand supply to replay a fixed sequence to each subscriber, and a live supply (via a `Supplier`) to broadcast events as they happen.

pages.title: Live supplies in action

blocks.v: Because a live supply broadcasts to whatever taps are listening at the moment, several listeners can follow the same stream at once — and each is free to join or leave whenever it likes. Here two listeners watch a stream of events: a `log` that records everything, and an `alert` that joins later and leaves earlier.
This prints:

log:   start
log:   warning
alert: warning
log:   all clear
alert: all clear
alert: stop
The lifecycle of the two taps lines up like this — 🟢 marks a tap joining, 🔴 a tap leaving, and ✅ each value a tap actually receives:
A blank cell means that tap was not listening when the value went out. Follow the timeline:

items: `.tap` returns a **`Tap` object** — the handle you keep to control that one subscription.

`start` is emitted while only `log` is listening, so only `log` sees it. This is the live-supply rule again: `alert` joined *after* `start`, and a live supply does not replay the past, so `alert` never sees it.
`warning` and `all clear` are emitted while **both** are tapped, so each value reaches both — in the order the taps subscribed, `log` first, then `alert`.
Calling `$log.close` **leaves** the supply. From then on `log` receives nothing, so the final `stop` reaches only `alert`.

blocks.v: Two things to take away. First, a single live supply can fan out to many independent taps at once. Second, each tap is its own subscription with its own lifetime: hold on to the `Tap` object that `.tap` returns, and you can end that one listener with `.close` without disturbing the others.

pages.title: react and whenever

blocks.v: Tapping a single supply is fine, but real reactive programs often watch **several** streams at once and react to whichever produces a value next. Raku has dedicated syntax for this: the `react` block, with one or more `whenever` blocks inside it.
A `react` block sets up the reactions and then waits, running each `whenever` body as its supply emits — until all the supplies are done. This section shows how the two work together.

prompt.v: Using a `react` block with a single `whenever`, collect the values of a supply built from the strings `'a'`, `'b'`, `'c'`, pushing each one **upper-cased** into an array. Print the array after the react block finishes.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The `whenever` body runs once per value, upper-casing it and pushing it onto `@collected`.
`react` waits for the single supply to finish, so by the time `say` runs the array holds all three values in order: `[A B C]`.

A supply has list-like methods of its own, so you could upper-case in the stream instead of in the body — `whenever Supply.from-list('a', 'b', 'c').map(*.uc) { @collected.push($_) }` — and the effect is the same. `.map` on a supply transforms each value as it flows past; the choice is simply whether the transformation belongs to the stream or to the reaction.

prompt.v: Using a `react` block, split one stream into two collections. Watch a supply built from `4, 42, 7, 100, 15` and, inside the `whenever` body, push every value greater than `10` into `@big` and the rest into `@small`. Print both arrays after the react block finishes.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The `whenever` body is ordinary code, so it can do more than collect — here it **decides**, routing each value to `@big` or `@small` as it arrives. Within each array the values keep their stream order.
The react block waits until the stream is done, so both arrays are complete before they are printed.

prompt.v: Track a bank balance fed by two streams with **opposite roles**. Create two named supplies — deposits from `100, 50, 200` and withdrawals from `30, 120` — and, in one `react` block with two `whenever` blocks, **add** every deposit to the balance and **subtract** every withdrawal from it. Print the final balance.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The two `whenever` blocks watch the two named supplies and react **differently**: deposits are added, withdrawals subtracted. One react block, two streams, two distinct reactions — that is the point of having a `whenever` per source.

The react block finishes only when both supplies are done, so the balance is final before it is printed: `100 + 50 + 200 - 30 - 120` gives `200`. Since addition and subtraction commute, the interleaving of the two streams does not affect the result.

Here both supplies deliver their values instantly, one stream after the other. In real life the events of a bank account arrive spread out over time — a deposit now, a withdrawal an hour later — and the two streams interlace, as in the [Two timers](/paradigms/react-whenever/two-timers) demo. The code stays exactly the same: the react block runs whichever `whenever` body matches each event as it comes in.

pages.title: The react block

blocks.v: A `react` block is a place where reactions live. Inside it, a `whenever` says “whenever this supply emits a value, run this body”. The `react` block then waits until every supply it watches is finished:
The `whenever` body runs once for each value — `1`, `2`, `3` — adding it to `$sum`. The topic value is available as `$_` (you can also name it with `-> $v`).

The key behaviour is that `react` **blocks** until its supplies are done. Only after the `Supply.from-list` has emitted all its values does the `react` block finish and the program move on to the `say`. That is why `$sum` is already `6` by the time it is printed: the react block waited for the whole stream.
This makes `react` a natural place to gather results from a stream: set up the reactions, let it run to completion, and use what you collected afterwards.

prompt.v: What does the following program print?

explanation.v: The `whenever` body collects each value, but calls `done` as soon as it sees `3`. `done` closes the `react` block, so the supply is abandoned and `4` and `5` are never processed, leaving `[1 2 3]`.

pages.title: whenever

blocks.v: A single `react` block can hold **several** `whenever` blocks, each watching a different supply. The block reacts to whichever supply emits next, running the matching body:
Both supplies are watched at once. Their values — `1, 2, 3` and `10, 20` — all flow into `$sum`, which ends at `36`. The `react` block finishes only when **both** supplies are done.

Each `whenever` reacts independently, so this is how you combine streams: one `whenever` per source, all inside the same `react`. A real program might watch a network connection in one `whenever` and a timer in another, responding to each as its events arrive.
Within a `whenever` body you have the emitted value (as `$_` or a named parameter) and can do anything with it — update state, emit to another supply, or even close the react block early with `done`.

prompt.v: What does the following program print?

explanation.v: The `whenever` body runs for each value, pushing twice its value. The supply emits `1, 2, 3`, so `@out` collects `2, 4, 6`.

prompt.v: What does the following program print?

explanation.v: The first `whenever` pushes `1`, then `2` — and on `2` it calls `done`. The crucial point is that `done` ends the **entire `react` block**, not just its own `whenever`: the rest of the first supply (`3`) and the *whole second supply* (`10, 20`) are cut off before they are delivered. So `@out` holds just `[1 2]`. If `done` only silenced its own stream, you would have seen `[1 2 10 20]` — but one `done` stops all the reactions at once.

pages.title: Supplies defined outside

blocks.v: Every `whenever` so far has created its supply right there in the header — `whenever Supply.from-list(...)`. That reads well for a quick example, but real programs rarely have their event source on hand at exactly that spot. More often a supply is built somewhere else — returned by a function, produced by a `Supplier`, or handed to you by a socket or a timer — and arrives as a plain variable. A `whenever` is just as happy to watch a named supply:
This prints:

temperature: 18
temperature: 21
temperature: 19
message: hi
message: bye

So read `whenever $sensors { … }` as “whenever the `$sensors` supply — wherever it came from — emits a value, run this body”. The inline `whenever Supply.from-list(...)` you saw earlier is just the special case where the source happens to be created on the spot.
If this outer-block-with-inner-blocks shape reminds you of something, you are right — the [next page](/paradigms/react-whenever/whenever-vs-when) compares it with `given`/`when`.

pages.title: whenever vs when

blocks.v: The shape of a `react` block may look familiar. An outer block holding several inner blocks, each acting on the topic `$_`, is exactly how [`given`/`when`](/advanced/given-when) is written. If you had a single temperature reading instead of a whole stream of them, you would branch on it like this:
The resemblance to `react`/`whenever` is real, but the two do very different jobs:

items: **`given`/`when` handles one value, right now.** `given` sets `$_` to a single value; each `when` tests it (`$_ ~~ 18`), the **first** match runs, and the block is finished. It is an ordinary, synchronous conditional.

**`react`/`whenever` handles many values, over time.** A `whenever` does not test `$_` against a pattern — it *subscribes* to a supply, and its body runs for **every** value that supply emits, whenever that value arrives. All the `whenever`s are live at once, and `react` keeps blocking until each of their supplies is finished.

blocks.v: So `when` asks “does this one value match?”, while `whenever` says “for each value this stream ever produces, do this”. Same skeleton, very different lives: a branch taken a single time, versus a reaction that runs again and again as events arrive.

pages.title: Two timers

blocks.v: Every react example so far has used `Supply.from-list`, which pushes all of its values the instant it is tapped. That is why each stream printed in full before the next one started — there was no waiting involved. Real event streams are not like that: their values arrive spread out over **time**, and a `react` block interleaves them as they come.

A timer is the simplest stream that behaves this way. `Supply.interval($period)` emits an increasing counter — `0, 1, 2, …` — once every `$period` seconds. Run two of them at different rates inside one `react`, and their values weave together:
A typical run prints:

tick 0
TOCK 0
tick 1
tick 2
TOCK 1
tick 3
tick 4
TOCK 2

The fast `tick` fires every `0.3` seconds; the slower `TOCK` every `0.5`, starting a quarter-second in (the second argument to `interval` is that initial delay). Neither waits for the other — the `react` block just runs whichever `whenever` body goes with the value that has arrived, so the two streams **intersect** instead of taking turns.

Because timers never finish on their own, a third `whenever` provides the exit: `Promise.in(1.4)` is kept after 1.4 seconds, and its body calls `done` to end the `react` block. Without it, the react would tick and tock forever.

The exact interleaving depends on timing, so a later run may order the lines a little differently — but that is the nature of reacting to live events: you respond to each as it happens, whenever it happens.

pages.title: await

blocks.v: Concurrent and reactive code launches work that finishes later. At some point you need to **wait** for that work and use its result. The tool for this is `await`.

You have already met `await` with [promises](/paradigms/promises). This section gathers the idea together: how `await` waits for one or many promises, and how reactive constructs like `react` provide the same “wait until done” guarantee for streams.

prompt.v: Start **three** promises: one that sleeps `0.3` seconds and produces the string `'slow'`, one that sleeps `0.1` and produces `'quick'`, and one that sleeps `0.2` and produces `'medium'`. Await them all as a list and print the results. Note what order they come back in: the quick job finishes first, but does that change the output?

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: All three jobs start at once and sleep concurrently, so the whole program takes about `0.3` seconds — the duration of the slowest job, not the sum of all three.

Although `quick` finishes first and `slow` last, the output is `(slow quick medium)`: `await` returns each result at the same position as its promise in `@jobs`. Completion order affects only *when* `await` returns, never the arrangement of the results.

prompt.v: `await` accepts more than promises — a supply can be awaited too: the program waits until the stream is **done** and gets its **last** value back. Build a supply of sensor readings from `18, 21, 19, 23`, await it, and print the final reading in the form shown below. No `tap` and no `react` block — a single `await` does the waiting.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Awaiting a supply blocks until the stream has emitted everything it has — the same “wait until complete” that `await` gives for a promise — and its value is the **last** thing the supply emitted, `23`.
This suits a stream where only the end state matters, like the latest sensor reading. If you need *every* value, that is a job for `.tap` or a `react` block, as in the previous sections.

prompt.v: When a promise’s block throws, `await` rethrows that exception at the point of the `await`. Start a promise whose block does `die 'boom'`. Await it inside a `try` block with a `CATCH` phaser that prints `caught: <message>`.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The promise’s block throws, so the promise is *broken*. The exception is not lost — it is held until someone awaits the promise.
`await $p` rethrows it right there, where the `CATCH` phaser handles it like any ordinary exception. This is how errors in background work surface where you wait for the result.

pages.title: Awaiting a promise

blocks.v: `await` takes a promise, waits for it to complete, and returns its result:

my $p = start { 7 * 6 };
say await $p; # 42
The program pauses at `await` only as long as needed, then continues with the value the promise produced.
Given several promises, `await` waits for **all** of them and returns their results in the same order as the promises in the list:

The jobs run concurrently, but `await @jobs` does not return until every one is done. Each result then sits at the same position as its promise in `@jobs` — no matter which job happened to finish first.

If an awaited promise was **broken** — its block threw an exception — `await` rethrows that exception at the point of the `await`. This means errors in background work surface where you wait for it, so you can handle them with the usual `try` / `CATCH` from the part on exceptions:
This prints:
the job failed: no such file

The `die` happens on a background thread, but the exception travels with the promise and pops out at `await`. The `try` catches it there, leaving `$result` undefined and the error in `$!` — so a failure in concurrent work is handled exactly like any other exception. Awaiting is therefore not just about getting a value; it is the moment where concurrent work rejoins the main flow, results and errors alike.

prompt.v: What does the following program print?

explanation.v: `await` waits for the single promise to finish and returns its result. The block computes `8 * 8`, so `await $p` is `64`.

prompt.v: What does the following program do?

options.text: Prints `waiting` at once, then prints `42` about two seconds later
Pauses for two seconds, then prints `waiting` and `42` together
Prints `waiting` and `42` at once — the sleep happens in the background
Prints `waiting`, then `Promise` — you cannot await a sleeping promise

explanation.v: `start` returns a promise **immediately** — the block, with its `sleep`, runs on a background thread. So `say 'waiting'` executes straight away. It is `await` that blocks: the program pauses there until the background block finishes its two-second nap and produces `42`, which is then printed. The pause belongs to the `await` line, not to the `start` line.

pages.title: Waiting for completion

blocks.v: `await` is the explicit way to wait, but reactive code waits too — just implicitly. A `react` block does not finish until all the supplies it watches are done, which gives you the same “everything has completed” guarantee:
The `say` runs only **after** the react block has finished, so `@values` already holds every emitted value. In effect, the `react` block awaited the stream for you.

This is a useful pattern: use a `react` block to collect everything a supply emits, and then work with the collected result on the line after, confident that the stream is complete. Whether you wait for a promise with `await` or for a stream with `react`, the principle is the same — pause until the concurrent work is done, then continue with its results.

pages.title: Making remote connections

blocks.v: The last subpart of the course turns to _web_ programming — talking to other machines over the network. We build up from the bottom: a raw network connection, then a simple HTTP client, a simple HTTP server, and finally a glimpse of the Cro framework.

Unlike the rest of the course, these examples need a **network connection** to run, and the later ones need modules you install yourself. The code is written to compile and to work when you run it against a real server, but its output cannot be shown the way the offline examples can. Each page notes what it needs.
We begin with the foundation of all network code: a _socket_, the two-way pipe between two programs across a network.

prompt.v: Try to open a TCP socket to `example.com` on port `80`, but guard the attempt with `try` so a failure does not crash the program. If the connection succeeds, print `connected to example.com` and close the socket; otherwise print `could not connect to example.com`.
This exercise needs a working network connection to actually connect.
When the connection succeeds, the program prints:

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `IO::Socket::INET.new(:host, :port)` opens the connection immediately, and throws if the host is unreachable.

Wrapping it in `try` turns that exception into a `Nil` instead of a crash. The `if … -> $conn` binds the socket when the connection succeeds and runs the `else` branch when it does not — the robust way to attempt a connection.

To see the `else` branch in action, change `$host` to a name that does not exist, such as `'example.comp'`. The DNS lookup then fails — without the `try` you would get an error like `Failed to resolve host name 'example.comp'` — but here the `try` turns it into `Nil`, so the program calmly prints `could not connect to example.comp`.

prompt.v: Open a socket to `example.com` on port `80`, send a minimal HTTP **HEAD** request (which asks only for the headers, not the page body), receive the reply, and print its first line (the status line).
This exercise needs a working network connection to run.
When run, the program prints a line such as:

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `.print` sends the request; the protocol lines end in `\r\n`. A `HEAD` request asks the server for just the status line and headers, so the reply is small.
`.recv` reads the reply, and `.lines.first` takes its first line — the HTTP status line.

pages.title: Opening a socket

blocks.v: A _socket_ is a connection between two programs over a network. Raku’s core class for TCP sockets is `IO::Socket::INET`, and you need nothing extra installed to use it.
To connect to a remote server, create a socket with the host and port you want to reach:

`IO::Socket::INET.new` opens the connection straight away. Port `80` is the standard port for HTTP, so this connects to the web server at `raku.org`. When you are finished, `.close` releases the connection.
This example needs a working network connection to run. When it connects successfully it prints `connected`.

The same class is used in two modes: as a **client**, connecting out to a server as shown here, and as a **server**, listening for connections coming in (which you will see later). For now, the idea to take away is that `IO::Socket::INET.new(:host, :port)` gives you a live two-way channel to another machine.

prompt.v: Which core Raku class opens a TCP network connection?

explanation.v: `IO::Socket::INET` is the core class for TCP sockets. It works both as a client (connecting to a server) and as a server (listening for connections), and needs no extra modules.

pages.title: Sending and receiving

blocks.v: Once a socket is open, you exchange data through it. Send text with `.print`, and read what comes back with `.recv`:
This sends a minimal HTTP request and reads the server’s reply into `$response`. The first line of a reply from a web server is its status line.

This example needs a working network connection. When run, it prints the reply’s status line. Because `raku.org` redirects plain HTTP to the secure HTTPS site, that line is a redirect, such as `HTTP/1.1 308 Permanent Redirect`, rather than `200 OK`. The special domain `example.com` does not redirect, so aiming the same request there prints a plain `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` instead.

Two details matter when talking to servers. First, network protocols usually separate lines with `
` (carriage return plus newline), not a plain `
`, which is why the request is written with `
`. Second, `.recv` returns whatever data has arrived so far; for larger replies you read in a loop until the connection closes.
Sending bytes and receiving bytes is all a socket really does. Everything else — HTTP, and the higher-level tools in the coming sections — is built on top of this simple send-and-receive.

prompt.v: In an HTTP request sent over a socket, what marks the end of the request headers?

explanation.v: HTTP separates the headers from the body — and signals “no more headers” — with a blank line, written as an extra `\r\n`. Without it, the server keeps waiting for the rest of the request.

pages.title: A simple HTTP server

blocks.v: A _server_ is the other side of a connection: instead of reaching out to a remote machine, it waits for clients to reach **in**. The same core class, `IO::Socket::INET`, does this too — you just put it in listening mode.

This section builds a tiny web server by hand: listen for a connection, read the request, and send back an HTTP response. Like the socket examples earlier, these need to be run on your own machine and connected to with a browser or another program.

prompt.v: Make the server do real work with the client's input, rather than returning a fixed string. Write a server that, in a **loop** (as on the previous page), reads each request, takes the requested **path**, and sends it back **upper-cased** — so a request for `/hello` replies with `HELLO`. The path is the second word of the request's first line (`GET /hello HTTP/1.0`); drop the leading `/` before upper-casing it. It keeps serving request after request; stop it with Ctrl-C.
Requesting a path with `curl` returns it in capitals:

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `.recv` reads the request. Its first line is `GET /hello HTTP/1.0`; `.words[1]` picks out `/hello`, and `.substr(1)` drops the leading slash to leave `hello`.
`.uc` upper-cases it, and that becomes the response body. The reply now depends on what the client asked for — the server is **processing** the request, not returning a fixed string.
The whole accept-read-respond block sits inside a `loop`, so the server answers one request after another instead of stopping after the first. Stop it with Ctrl-C.

pages.title: Listening for connections

blocks.v: To act as a server, create a socket in **listening** mode with the `:listen` argument, giving the address and port to listen on:
`:localhost('127.0.0.1')` listens on your own machine, and `:localport(8080)` is the port clients must connect to. The socket is now waiting, but no client has arrived yet.
To take the next incoming connection, call `.accept`. It **blocks** until a client connects, then returns a fresh socket representing that one conversation:

my $conn = $listener.accept;
say 'a client connected';
The `$listener` keeps listening for more clients, while `$conn` is your channel to talk to this particular one. A real server calls `.accept` in a loop, handling each client as it arrives.
These examples run on your own machine; connect to them from a browser or another program at `127.0.0.1:8080`.
So a server is just a socket turned around: instead of `:host`/`:port` to dial out, you give `:listen` with `:localhost`/`:localport` to wait for calls in.

prompt.v: Which argument makes `IO::Socket::INET` wait for incoming connections instead of dialling out to a server?

explanation.v: `:listen` puts the socket in server mode, waiting on a local address and port. You then call `.accept` to take each incoming connection. (`.accept` is a method, not a constructor argument.)

pages.title: Responding to a request

blocks.v: Once a client has connected, you read its request and send a response. For a web browser, the response must be valid HTTP: a status line, optional headers, a blank line, and then the body.

The response mirrors the request format you saw on the client side. `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` is the status line, `Content-Type: text/plain` is a header, the blank line (`\r\n\r\n`) ends the headers, and `Hello, web!` is the body the browser displays.
Run this program, then hit it from another terminal with `curl` (or open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` in a browser), and it prints the body straight to the screen:

$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
Hello, web!

This handles a single request and then stops. To serve many requests, you would wrap the `.accept`-read-respond steps in a loop, and typically handle each connection on its own thread or promise so that slow clients do not block the others. But the essence of a web server is exactly this: accept a connection, read the request, write an HTTP response.
The [next page](/paradigms/http-server/serving-requests) does exactly that — a server that stays alive, looping to answer one request after another instead of stopping after the first.

pages.title: Serving many requests

blocks.v: The server on the previous page handled a single request and then stopped. A real server keeps running, answering client after client. Wrap the accept-read-respond steps in a `loop` — and because the loop shares the variables declared around it, you can keep state between requests. Here the server counts its customers and tells each one their number:

`.accept` **blocks** until a client connects, then returns a fresh socket for that one conversation. Because `$customer` lives outside the loop, it survives from one request to the next: the first visitor is customer `1`, the second `2`, and so on. The loop never ends on its own, so the server stays up until you stop it with Ctrl-C.
Two details are worth noticing:

items: **The response is written in two parts.** The first `.print` sends the HTTP header — the status line, the content type, and the blank line that ends the headers. The second sends the body. HTTP does not care whether these arrive in one write or several, so splitting them keeps the fixed protocol boilerplate apart from the part that actually changes.

**The body comes from a template.** `qq:to/END/` is a *heredoc* — a `qq` string that runs to the line `END`. It spans several lines and interpolates `$customer` just like any double-quoted string, which makes it a neat little templating tool for building a reply. (It is one of the [quoting constructs](/advanced/quoting-constructs) from earlier in the course.)

blocks.v: Connect a few times to watch the counter climb:

$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
Hello!
You are customer number 1.
Thanks for visiting.
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
Hello!
You are customer number 2.
Thanks for visiting.

Handling requests one after another like this is the simplest kind of server. A production server would also serve each connection on its own thread or promise, so a slow client cannot hold up the others — but the heart of it is exactly this loop: accept, read, respond, repeat.

pages.title: Cro 101

blocks.v: Building real web services on raw sockets quickly becomes tedious: parsing requests, routing URLs, handling many clients, speaking HTTPS. **Cro** is the Raku framework that does all of this for you. It is the standard, modern way to write web servers and clients in Raku.
This final section is a short tour of Cro — just enough to see its shape. Cro is not part of the core, so to run these examples you install it first with `zef install cro`.

prompt.v: Extend the greeting service with a **second** route: a `GET` route for the path `bye` that returns the plain text `Goodbye!`. Keep the original `hello` route as well.
This exercise needs Cro installed (`zef install cro`).

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: A `route` block can hold as many routes as you like; each `get` handles one path.
Cro matches the request path to the right route, so `/hello` and `/bye` return their own responses.

As on the theory page, `.start` returns immediately, so the closing `react` block keeps the program alive until you press Ctrl-C — `whenever signal(SIGINT)` then stops the server and ends the reaction.

prompt.v: Fetch a web page's status the easy way — with the **Cro client module** instead of a raw socket. Use `Cro::HTTP::Client.get` to fetch `http://example.com/`, `await` the response, and print its `.status` — no text parsing needed.
This exercise needs the Cro module installed (`zef install cro`) and a working network connection.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `Cro::HTTP::Client.get` returns a promise — a network request finishes later — so we `await` it.

The response object already knows its `.status`, so we get `200` directly, without sending the request text or parsing the reply by hand. Compare this with the raw-socket version: the module does all the protocol work for you.

pages.title: What is Cro

blocks.v: Cro is a set of libraries for building **services** — programs that talk to other programs over the network. It is best known for HTTP, but it also handles WebSockets, and it builds everything on the reactive tools from earlier in this part: [supplies](/paradigms/supplies), `react`, and `whenever`. A Cro request handler is, at heart, a reaction to a stream of incoming requests. Its home site, with the full documentation and examples, is [cro.services](https://cro.services).
What Cro gives you over raw sockets:

items: **Routing** — map URL paths to the code that handles them, instead of parsing requests by hand.
**Request and response objects** — read query parameters and send JSON without assembling text.
**Concurrency** — many clients are served at once, on the thread pool, automatically.
**Composability** — services are built from small pieces you can test and combine.

blocks.v: You install it from the ecosystem:
zef install cro

Cro is a big framework with many dependencies, so this takes a few minutes. If the installation stops on a dependency identity it cannot find — an error mentioning something like `JSON::Fast:ver<0.19+>:auth<cpan:TIMOTIMO>` — your copy of `zef` is too old to know the archive that serves such historical module identities. Upgrade the installer itself with `zef install zef`, open a fresh terminal, and run the Cro installation again.

Cro brings the whole course together: object-oriented design for its types, the functional style in its handlers, and the reactive model for its streams of requests. The next topic shows the smallest possible Cro service so you can see how those ideas come together in real web code.

pages.title: A Cro route

blocks.v: A Cro HTTP service is described by a set of _routes_: each route says which URL it handles and what to return. You build them inside a `route` block with the `get` keyword:

Read the route as “a `GET` request for the path `hello` returns the text `Hello from Cro!`”. The `content` function sets both the content type and the body — no manual status lines or `\r\n` in sight. `Cro::HTTP::Server` ties the routes to an address and port, and `.start` begins serving.

One subtlety: `.start` does **not** block — it starts the service on background threads and returns at once, and if the program simply ended there, the server would vanish with it. The closing `react` block is what keeps the program alive, and it is an old friend: `whenever signal(SIGINT)` reacts to the interrupt signal (Ctrl-C on the keyboard) by stopping the server and calling `done`. The reactive tools from earlier in this part are exactly how a Cro program waits, serves, and shuts down cleanly.
This example needs Cro installed (`zef install cro`). Run it, open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello`, and stop the server with Ctrl-C when you are done.

Do not worry if the server occasionally prints `Cannot write to a closed socket` while you browse. That is not a bug in your code: a client — typically a browser — opened a connection and dropped it before reading the reply, as browsers routinely do with speculative or cancelled requests. Cro notes the vanished client, and the server keeps serving.

A route can take URL segments as parameters, return JSON, and much more, but the shape is always this: declare what each path does, hand the routes to a server, and start it. Compared with the raw socket server of the previous section, Cro removes all the protocol bookkeeping and lets you write only the part that is specific to your service.
This route always says the same thing, though. The next page lets a route read a **parameter** from the URL, so a single route can greet `/hello/Anna` and `/hello/Bob` differently.

pages.title: A route with a parameter

blocks.v: The route on the previous page always returned the same text. Real services vary their reply by what the client asks for, and the simplest way is to read part of the **URL** as a parameter. In a Cro route, a segment after the fixed path becomes a variable in the signature:

The interesting part is the signature `-> 'hello', $name`: it matches a path of two segments — the literal `hello`, then anything, captured into `$name`. The rest of the program is the same server scaffolding as on the previous page. A request for `/hello/Anna` binds `$name` to `Anna` and returns `Hello, Anna!`; `/hello/Bob` returns `Hello, Bob!`. One route, a different answer for every name:

$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello/Anna
Hello, Anna!
This example needs Cro installed (`zef install cro`).

Parameters are how a route stays small while handling a whole family of paths. A route can take several segments, match only certain shapes, read query strings, and return JSON — but it all builds on this one idea: name the varying parts of the URL in the signature, and use them in the response.

Paths that match no route at all are not your problem: Cro answers them with `404 Not Found` on its own. And when a route *matches* but cannot deliver — the name looks up nothing, say — call `not-found` inside the handler to send that same 404 deliberately. The **method** is checked just as strictly as the path: this block only declares `get`, so a `HEAD` or `POST` request to the same path is answered with `405 Method Not Allowed`. You can see it yourself with `curl -I`, which sends `HEAD` rather than `GET`.
A service is only half the picture, though — something has to call it. The next page turns Cro around and uses its **client** to talk to a server like the ones you have just built.

pages.title: Using a client module

blocks.v: Cro is not only for building services — it also ships an HTTP **client** for making requests. The clearest way to meet it is to point it at the very server you built on the previous page. Here both halves run in one program: we start the service, then call it ourselves.

`Cro::HTTP::Client.get` returns a promise — fitting, since a network request finishes later — so you `await` it. The response object knows its status, headers, and body; `await $response.body-text` hands back the text the server sent, `Hello from Cro!`. Compare this with the raw socket of the [connections section](/paradigms/connections/sending-receiving): there is no `\r\n`, no status line to parse, no reading in a loop — the client and the server speak to each other in a few plain lines.
This example needs Cro installed (`zef install cro`).
When the page is not there

What if you ask for a path the service does not have? The server side is easy: a request that matches no route gets a `404 Not Found` from Cro automatically. On the client side, a failed request **throws** — the error travels with the promise and pops out at `await`, just as you saw with [broken promises](/paradigms/await/awaiting-promises) — so you handle it with the usual exception tools:

Our service has a `hello` route but no `goodbye`, so this prints `Request failed with status 404`. The exception carries the full response in its `.response`, with the status code and headers there to inspect.
Your own service is just the nearest server there is, though. The next page points the same client at the wider web — **public APIs** that answer with JSON or terminal-ready text.

pages.title: Fetching from a public API

blocks.v: The client from the previous page reaches any server on the web, not only your own. Many public APIs reply with JSON, and Cro parses that for you, so `.body` gives back a ready-made data structure rather than text. Here we ask a free weather service for the current temperature in Berlin:
which prints something like:

Berlin right now:
  temperature: 21.9 °C
  wind speed:  8.4 km/h

The exact numbers change with the weather, of course. The two numbers in the URL are geographic coordinates — `52.52° N, 13.41° E` is Berlin — so put your own city's latitude and longitude there to get your local weather. Either way, one request and `.body` (or `.body-text`) gives you the answer — no sockets, no status parsing, no JSON handling by hand.
Plain text for the terminal

JSON is not the only shape an answer can take. The weather service [wttr.in](https://wttr.in) can serve JSON too, but its speciality is plain text drawn for the terminal — and it decides the format by looking at **who is asking**: command-line clients get text, browsers get a web page. Cro lets you set request headers, so introduce yourself as one of the terminal folk:
This prints a one-line weather report, ready for a shell prompt or a status bar:
Berlin: 🌤️  +25°C
Here the body is plain text, so it is read with `.body-text`. Drop the `?format=3` from the URL and the service replies with its full, multi-line ASCII-art weather report instead.
These examples need Cro installed (`zef install cro`) and a working network connection.
Requests and responses are not the whole story, though. The final topic opens a **WebSocket** — a live, two-way channel where the reactive tools of this part get their grand finale.

pages.title: WebSockets

blocks.v: An HTTP conversation is one-shot: the client asks, the server answers, and the connection is done. A **WebSocket** upgrades that into a long-lived, two-way channel — either side can send a message at any moment, which is what chats, games, and live dashboards need. Cro supports WebSockets out of the box, and a WebSocket handler is built from the reactive tools you already know: a message stream is a supply.

Here is a tiny chat server. Every message any client sends is upper-cased by the server and broadcast to everyone connected — so what comes back is visibly *not* what went out, proving the data really made the round trip:

Look at the `web-socket` block — it is the reactive part of the course in miniature. Each connected client gets a `supply` with two `whenever`s: one watches `$incoming`, the messages arriving *from* that client, upper-cases each and pushes it into the shared `$chat` supplier; the other watches `$chat` and `emit`s every broadcast text back *to* the client. One `Supplier`, tapped by every connection, is the entire chat room.

The little `LAST { done }` matters. It is the [phaser](/advanced/block-phasers) you met with loops; in a `whenever` block it fires when the watched stream **ends** — that is, when this client disconnects. Calling `done` there closes the whole connection supply, unsubscribing it from `$chat`. Without it, a departed client's `whenever $chat` would linger, and the next broadcast would try to write to a closed socket and print an error on the server.
A browser talks to this with a few lines of JavaScript, but so does another Raku program — Cro also provides the client side:

`.send` fires the message off and returns at once; the reply arrives later, on another thread, in the `.tap` block. The main line must therefore wait before closing — and rather than sleeping and hoping, it awaits a `Promise` that the tap keeps the moment the reply lands: the concurrency tools from earlier in this part, doing exactly what they were made for.
Run the server in one terminal and this client in another. The client prints both directions of the conversation:

Sending:  Hello, chat!
Received: HELLO, CHAT!

What went out lowercase came back in capitals — the message travelled *to* the server, was transformed there, and travelled *back* over the same connection. That is the two-way channel in action. Start the client in several terminals at once and every message appears in all of them: a working chat in under thirty lines of Raku.
These examples need Cro installed (`zef install cro`).

This is a fitting place to end the course. A service, the client that calls it, and a live two-way channel between them stand on everything that came before — objects and exceptions, regexes and grammars, and the functional, concurrent, and reactive tools of this part — yet the code stays short and says exactly what you mean. From [bytes on a socket](/paradigms/connections/sending-receiving) to a chat room in a screenful of code: that is Raku.

pages.title: The Final Test

blocks.v: A hundred questions across the whole course, Parts 1 through 5, in roughly the order you learnt them. Each one is checked the moment you answer: you see at once whether you were right — and why — but you cannot change an answer or step back, only move forward. At the end you get your score and a link you can keep to share your result or review what you missed.

finalTest.q: In this course, `Raku` is the name of the programming language and `Rakudo` is the name of the compiler.
finalTest.explain: Raku is the language; Rakudo is the compiler (running on MoarVM).

finalTest.q: Which of these lines correctly print `Hello, World!` (with or without a trailing newline)?
finalTest.explain: Raku uses `say`/`put`/`print`, and routines like `say` can be called as methods; there is no `echo` routine.

finalTest.q: Which built-in routine reads a line of input from the user and returns it as a string? Type its name.
finalTest.explain: The `prompt` routine waits for input and returns it as a string.

finalTest.q: A single-line comment in Raku starts with `//` and continues to the end of the line.
finalTest.explain: A single-line comment starts with `#`, not `//` — in Raku `//` is the defined-or operator, not a comment.

finalTest.q: Which two-character combination begins a multi-line (or embedded) comment, before its enclosing brackets? Type it exactly.
finalTest.explain: Multi-line and embedded comments start with a `#` followed by a backtick and then a bracket pair such as `( )` or `{ }`.

finalTest.q: Which declarator introduces a new lexical variable, as in `___ $name;`? Type the keyword.
finalTest.explain: Variables are declared with the `my` declarator.

finalTest.q: In Raku, variable names (identifiers) are case insensitive, so `$name` and `$Name` refer to the same variable.
finalTest.explain: Identifiers are case sensitive: `$name`, `$Name`, and `$NAME` are three different variables.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The defined-or operator `//` returns the right operand when the left one is undefined.

finalTest.q: Which operator concatenates two strings in Raku? Type the single character.
finalTest.explain: The tilde `~` is the string concatenation operator.

finalTest.q: What does this print?
finalTest.explain: The `chars` method counts characters; this Chinese greeting has 4 characters (its byte count is 12).

finalTest.q: Variables are interpolated inside single-quoted strings but NOT inside double-quoted strings.
finalTest.explain: It is the other way round: double quotes interpolate variables and code, while single quotes show the characters as-is.

finalTest.q: What is printed?
options: `One\nTwo` on one line, then `Three` and `Four` on two lines
`One` and `Two` on two lines, then `Three` and `Four` on two lines
finalTest.explain: In single quotes `\n` is literal; in double quotes `\n` becomes a newline.

finalTest.q: Select all valid ways to write integer literals in Raku.
finalTest.explain: Underscores may group digits, and a leading `-` is fine; commas are not separators and a number cannot end with `_`.

finalTest.q: What does Raku print?
finalTest.explain: Decimals like `0.1` are `Rat` (fractions), so the arithmetic is exact and the result is `0`.

finalTest.q: What type does the literal `0.5` have?
finalTest.explain: A decimal literal such as `0.5` is a rational number, of type `Rat`.

finalTest.q: Which operator tests divisibility, returning `True` if the left operand is divisible by the right (e.g. `10 __ 5`)? Type the operator.
finalTest.explain: The `%%` operator is the divisibility test; `10 %% 5` is `True`.

finalTest.q: What is the result of `-10 % 3` in Raku?
finalTest.explain: `$a % $b` equals `$a - $b * floor($a / $b)`, so `-10 % 3` is `2`.

finalTest.q: Which of these are correct Boolean literal values in Raku?
finalTest.explain: `True` and `False` are the only Boolean literals; `TRUE` is not one and `1` is an integer.

finalTest.q: What does this print?
finalTest.explain: `&&` returns the last argument when none is false; with two truthy strings it returns `World`.

finalTest.q: How many elements does the range `1 ..^ 5` generate?
finalTest.explain: The `^` excludes the upper endpoint, so the range is `1, 2, 3, 4` — four elements.

finalTest.q: Which operator checks whether a value matches (falls within) a range, as in `$v ___ $r`? Type it.
finalTest.explain: The smart-match operator `~~` tests a value against a range (and many other things).

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The inner `my $x` is a separate local variable; inside the block it is `42`, outside it stays `1`.

finalTest.q: Which statements about conditionals in Raku are correct?
options: `unless` cannot be followed by an `else` block
Parentheses around an `if` condition are required
finalTest.explain: It is `elsif`, `unless` takes no `else`, and the ternary is `?? !!`; parentheses around `if` conditions are optional.

finalTest.q: Which operator tests two strings for equality?
finalTest.explain: String comparison uses word operators; `eq` tests equality (`==` is for numbers).

finalTest.q: What does this print?
finalTest.explain: The `while` statement modifier subtracts 3 repeatedly (10→7→4→1) until the condition fails, leaving `1`.

finalTest.q: What does `42.WHAT` print?
finalTest.explain: The `WHAT` method reports the type in parentheses; `42` is `(Int)`.

finalTest.q: Match the prefix coercion operators. Which pairings are correct?
finalTest.explain: `~` is string, `+` is numeric, `?` is Boolean coercion; `!` is Boolean negation, not string coercion.

finalTest.q: Given `my Int $var = 42;`, the assignment `$var = '314E-2';` raises a type-check error.
finalTest.explain: A typed `Int` container rejects a `Str`, producing "Type check failed... expected Int but got Str".

finalTest.q: Which statements about arrays and hashes are correct?
options: The `elems` method returns an array's length
finalTest.explain: Arrays use `@`, hashes use `%`, `elems` gives the size, and indices start at `0`.

finalTest.q: What does this print?
finalTest.explain: A function returns its last evaluated value, so no explicit `return` is needed; this prints `30`.

finalTest.q: Which method does `say` use to turn a value into text?
finalTest.explain: `say` prints the human-friendly `.gist` form, while `print`/`put` use `.Str` and `dd`/REPL use `.raku`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: `.Str` joins the elements with spaces and drops the brackets, unlike `.gist` which shows `[1 2 3]`.

finalTest.q: The `dd` routine writes its output to standard output (STDOUT), the same stream as `say`.
finalTest.explain: `dd` is a debugging tool that dumps the `.raku` form of its arguments to standard error (STDERR), not STDOUT.

finalTest.q: Given `my Int $int;`, which assignment causes an error because Raku does no automatic casting?
finalTest.explain: Assigning the Rat `123.45` to an `Int` container fails; you must convert explicitly with `.Int`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: Arrays do not auto-flatten when nested, so `@c` holds two array elements.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: Binding with `:=` makes `$y` refer to the same container as `$x`, so changing `$x` changes `$y`.

finalTest.q: What does `say +@a` print for `my @a = 10, 20, 30;`?
finalTest.explain: Prefix `+` forces numeric context, and an array in numeric context becomes its element count (3).

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: `$( )` forces item context, so the array is one single item and the loop runs only once.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The `:delete` adverb removes the key from the hash and returns the value it held, so `$v` is `1` and only `b` remains.

finalTest.q: For `my %h = a => 1, b => 2;`, the expression `%h<z>:exists` returns `False`.
finalTest.explain: `:exists` asks whether the key is present, and there is no `z` key in the hash.

finalTest.q: Which twigil marks a dynamic variable that is looked up through the call stack (e.g. `$*OUT`)? Give just the twigil character.
finalTest.explain: The `*` twigil denotes a dynamic variable resolved through dynamic scope, unlike lexical variables.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: A dynamic variable is found through the call stack, so `show` sees the `$*n` set by its caller `run`.

finalTest.q: What does `say $x.WHAT` print for an untyped, unassigned `my $x;`?
finalTest.explain: An untyped variable starts as the `Any` type, and `.WHAT` prints the type object with parentheses.

finalTest.q: `.WHAT` returns a type object printed with parentheses like `(Int)`, while `.^name` returns a bare string like `Int`.
finalTest.explain: `.WHAT` yields the type object (shown as `(Int)`); `.^name` returns the name as a plain string.

finalTest.q: What does `say :3<12>;` print?
finalTest.explain: The radix form `:3<12>` reads 12 in base 3, giving 1*3 + 2 = 5.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: A sized native `int8` wraps around on overflow, so decrementing -128 rolls to 127.

finalTest.q: What does `say (set(1, 2) ∪ set(2, 3)).elems;` print?
finalTest.explain: The union is the distinct set {1, 2, 3}, which has 3 elements.

finalTest.q: What does `say 1, 3, 9 ... 81;` print?
finalTest.explain: Three seed values with a constant ratio make a geometric sequence multiplying by 3 up to 81.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.code:
enum Colour <red green blue>;
say green + blue;
finalTest.explain: Enum constants number from zero (red=0, green=1, blue=2), so green + blue is 1 + 2 = 3.

finalTest.q: Which of these produce `(11 22 33)` from `(1, 2, 3)` and `(10, 20, 30)`? (select all that apply)
finalTest.explain: Zip `Z+` and hyper `»+»` both add element-by-element; cross `X+` pairs every combination instead.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: Defining `infix:<times>` creates a new operator between two operands whose body multiplies them.

finalTest.q: A `BEGIN` phaser runs at run time, only after the whole program has finished compiling.
finalTest.explain: `BEGIN` fires at compile time, as early as possible — not at run time.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: `gather` collects only the values passed to `take`, and the guard is true only for 3 and 6.

finalTest.q: In `sub f($first, *@rest) {...}`, calling `f('a', 'b', 'c')` leaves `@rest` with 2 elements.
finalTest.explain: Fixed parameters fill first, so `$first` takes `a` and the slurpy `*@rest` collects the remaining two.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: In a subscript, bare `*` is the element count (5), so `*-2` is index 3, whose value is 8.

finalTest.q: Which method do you call on a class name to create a new instance (object) of that class?
finalTest.explain: An instance is created by calling the `new` method on the class name, e.g. `Dog.new`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: A type object is undefined (`False`), while an instance made with `new` is defined (`True`).

finalTest.q: Declaring an attribute with `has $.name` automatically creates a public accessor method called `name`.
finalTest.explain: The `$.` form both declares the attribute and generates a same-named accessor method.

finalTest.q: By default, the accessor generated by `has $.name` is read-only. Which trait makes it writable from outside?
finalTest.explain: Marking the attribute `is rw` makes its accessor return a writable container so assignment works.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: With no `weight` passed to `new`, the attribute takes its default of `4.0`, shown as `4`.

finalTest.q: Inside a method, which keyword refers to the object the method was called on?
finalTest.explain: The invocant object is available inside a method as `self`.

finalTest.q: An attribute declared with `has $!code` has no public accessor and cannot be read from outside the object.
finalTest.explain: The `$!` form declares a private attribute, reachable only inside the class’s own methods.

finalTest.q: The `new` method that creates objects is an instance method — you must already have an object before you can call it.
finalTest.explain: `new` is called on the class (the type object), not on an existing instance, so it is a class method.

finalTest.q: What is the key difference between a subroutine and a method?
options: A method belongs to a class and is called on an object with the dot; a subroutine stands alone and takes all data as arguments
A subroutine can return a value but a method cannot
A method cannot take parameters, a subroutine can
There is no difference; the keywords are interchangeable
finalTest.explain: A method is called on an object and uses its state via `self`; a sub stands alone and receives everything as arguments.

finalTest.q: Which trait, written after a class name, makes it inherit from a parent class (e.g. `class Dog ___ Animal`)?
finalTest.explain: `class Dog is Animal` makes `Dog` inherit the attributes and methods of `Animal`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The inherited `intro` calls `self.speak`, which resolves to the Dog’s overriding `speak`.

finalTest.q: Which of the following are true about roles? (Select all that apply.)
options: A role is given to a class with the `does` trait
A class can compose more than one role
A role describes something a class *can do*, rather than what it *is*
A role can only be used through inheritance with `is`
finalTest.explain: Roles are composed with `does` (one or several) and express capability; they are not applied via `is`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The `but Loud` mixin overrides `greet`; `callsame` runs the original and `.uc` upper-cases it.

finalTest.q: Which meta-method (written with the `.^` syntax) returns a type’s method resolution order / inheritance chain?
finalTest.explain: `.^mro` returns the method resolution order — the chain of types Raku searches.

finalTest.q: Which routine writes its text to standard error rather than standard output?
finalTest.explain: `note` writes to `$*ERR` (standard error); `say`, `print`, and `put` go to `$*OUT`.

finalTest.q: Which statements about `spurt` and `slurp` are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: `spurt` writes a string to a file, creating or replacing it
`slurp` reads a whole file’s contents into a string
Passing `:append` to `spurt` adds to the end instead of replacing
`slurp` deletes the file after reading it
finalTest.explain: `spurt` writes (with `:append` to add), `slurp` reads the whole file; neither deletes anything.

finalTest.q: `rmdir` will remove a directory even when it still contains files.
finalTest.explain: `rmdir` removes only an empty directory; a non-empty one is left untouched.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: A `Proc`’s `.exitcode` reports the program’s exit code, here `3`.

finalTest.q: After a `try` block catches an exception, what happens to the value the block evaluates to and to `$!`?
options: The block evaluates to an undefined value, and the caught exception is stored in `$!`
The block re-throws and the program stops
The block returns the exception message as a string, and `$!` is empty
finalTest.explain: A failed `try` block yields an undefined value while the caught exception is available in `$!`.

finalTest.q: What must a custom exception class do to be usable as an exception?
options: Inherit from `Exception` and provide a `message` method
Nothing special; any class can be thrown
finalTest.explain: A custom exception inherits from the built-in `Exception` class and supplies a `message` method, then is thrown with `.throw`.

finalTest.q: Inside a Raku regex, an unquoted space in the pattern is significant and must match a real space in the string.
finalTest.explain: By default spaces in a regex are insignificant and only aid readability; to match a real space you quote it or use `\s` (or turn on `:s`).

finalTest.q: To match any single character that is NOT in a set, which single symbol do you put right after the opening bracket, as in `<-[a..z]>`?
finalTest.explain: A minus sign after `<[` negates the character class, matching any character not listed.

finalTest.q: Which predefined character class matches a single digit?
finalTest.explain: `\d` matches a digit; `\w` is a word character, `\s` is whitespace, and `\D` is a non-digit.

finalTest.q: Which quantifier makes the item before it optional, matching it zero or one time?
finalTest.explain: `?` means zero or one occurrence; `*` is zero or more and `+` is one or more.

finalTest.q: What does this match?
finalTest.explain: The `?` after `+` makes it frugal, so `.+?` matches as little as possible and stops at the first `>`.

finalTest.q: After a successful match, which special variable holds the resulting Match object?
finalTest.explain: The match is stored in `$/`; individual captures are then available as `$0`, `$1`, and so on.

finalTest.q: How do you write a named capture called `age` around the sub-pattern `(\d+)`?
finalTest.explain: Raku names a capture with `$<name>=( … )`, reachable afterwards as `$<name>`.

finalTest.q: What does this match?
finalTest.explain: The single bar `|` uses longest-token matching, so it prefers the longer alternative `catdog` regardless of order.

finalTest.q: Wrapping a pattern in `^` and `$`, as in `/^ \d+ $/`, requires the pattern to match the entire string with nothing left over.
finalTest.explain: `^` anchors at the start and `$` at the end, so together they force a whole-string match.

finalTest.q: Which adverb added to `s///` (or `m///`) makes it replace or match every occurrence rather than only the first?
finalTest.explain: The `:g` (global) adverb applies the operation to every match instead of just the first.

finalTest.q: A `token` backtracks the same way a `regex` does when a later part of the pattern fails.
finalTest.explain: A `regex` backtracks, but a `token` does not — it commits to its match, which is why `token` is preferred in grammars.

finalTest.q: Which statements about `rule` in a grammar are true?
options: `rule` treats whitespace in the pattern as significant
`rule` behaves as if the `:s` adverb is on
`rule` is typically used for higher-level structure separated by spaces
finalTest.explain: A `rule` is a `token` (non-backtracking) with significant whitespace, equivalent to `:s`, and suits space-separated structure.

finalTest.q: Inside a token you call `make` to attach a value to the match. Which method (or its `.ast` alias) reads that value back afterwards?
finalTest.explain: `made` (alias `.ast`) retrieves the value stored on a match by `make`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The subroutine recurses down to the base case `$n <= 1`, computing 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: `adder(5)` returns a sub that adds 5, so `add5(3)` is 8 — the returned closure remembers `$n`.

finalTest.q: In Raku, a subroutine returned from another subroutine can keep using a variable from the enclosing scope even after that outer subroutine has finished.
finalTest.explain: That captured, persistent state is exactly what makes it a closure.

finalTest.q: Complete the reduction that concatenates a list of strings into one: `say [__] "a", "b", "c";` prints `abc`. Which operator goes in the brackets?
finalTest.explain: `[~]` reduces with the string-concatenation operator `~`, gluing the pieces into `abc`.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: The feed keeps the even numbers 2,4,6,8,10 then squares them to 4,16,36,64,100.

finalTest.q: What does `say (1, 1, * + * ... *)[^8];` print?
finalTest.explain: The closure `* + *` sums the two previous elements, giving the Fibonacci sequence; only the first eight are computed.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: Autothreading applies `+ 10` to each value of the any-junction, giving `any(11, 12, 13)`.

finalTest.q: You start a thread with `my $t = Thread.start({ ... });`. Which method do you call on `$t` to make the main program wait until that thread has completed? (give the method name, without dot or parentheses)
finalTest.explain: `.finish` (also spelled `.join`) blocks until the thread is done.

finalTest.q: What does this program print?
finalTest.explain: `.then` runs after `$p` completes; inside it `.result` is 10, doubled to 20.

finalTest.q: Calling `.list` on a channel returns immediately with whatever values are queued, without waiting for the channel to be closed.
finalTest.explain: `.list` blocks until the channel is closed, collecting every value; without a `.close` it would wait forever.

finalTest.q: Which of the following are true of a live supply created from a `Supplier` (as opposed to an on-demand supply like `Supply.from-list`)?
options: `A tap added after a value is emitted misses that earlier value`
`Each new tap replays the whole sequence from the start`
`Values are pushed to taps with .emit on the Supplier`
`It is the right model for real events such as clicks or messages`
finalTest.explain: A live supply broadcasts to current taps only and does not remember past values; replaying to every tap is on-demand behaviour.

finalTest.q: In a Cro `route` block, which function sets both the content type and the response body, so you never write a status line or `\r\n` by hand?
finalTest.explain: The `content` function sets the content type and body of a Cro response.

pages.title: Lists, arrays, and hashes

blocks.v: Exercises on shaping data: sorting and filtering lists, counting with hashes, combining structures, and using the zip metaoperator to line values up.

prompt.v: From the list `3, 9, 4, 9, 1, 7` find the second-largest *distinct* value and print it. (The two `9`s count as one, so the answer is `7`.)

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Turning the list into a `Set` with `.Set` throws away the duplicate `9`, since a

solution.v: set holds each value only once.

items: `.keys` gives the distinct values back — still `Int`s, not strings — so a plain

solution.v: `.sort` orders them numerically. The second-largest is then one place before the end, `[*-2]`.

prompt.v: Split the numbers `1` to `10` into two groups — even and odd — and print each group on its own line.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `* %% 2` is true for numbers divisible by two; `* % 2` is true when the

solution.v: remainder is non-zero, i.e. odd. Each `grep` keeps one group.

items: Interpolating `@even[]` with the empty-bracket zen slice prints the elements

prompt.v: Define a `Shape` role that requires an `area` method, then make `Circle` and `Square` classes that do the role.

Write a `describe` subroutine whose parameter is *typed* as `Shape`, so it accepts any shape and refuses anything that is not one. It should print the shape’s area labelled with its class name. Call it for a circle of radius `2` and a square of side `3`.

The subroutine never checks which kind of shape it received: because its parameter is a `Shape`, the object is guaranteed to have an `area` method, so the same `.area` call works on whichever shape comes in. That is what the role gives you — a single type you can require, and one piece of code that treats every class doing it uniformly.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Strictly, the call `$shape.area` would work *without* the role at all. Raku

solution.v: resolves methods by name at the moment of the call, so as long as each object happens to have an `area` method, the loop runs — this is known as *duck typing*. So what does the role actually buy us here? Two guarantees.

items: **The role is a type you can require.** `describe` is declared as

solution.v: `sub describe(Shape $shape)`, so it accepts only objects that do `Shape` and rejects anything else *before the body runs*. Pass it a plain number and the program refuses to compile:

describe(42);
    # Calling describe(Int) will never work with declared signature (Shape $shape)
Without the role there is no such type — a duck-typed routine would take any argument and only blow up later, deep inside, when it reaches `.area`.

items: **The role is a contract.** Declaring `area` as a stub (`method area { ... }`)

solution.v: forces every class that does the role to supply its own `area`. Forget it, and the mistake cannot go unnoticed:

Rakudo reports the missing method as soon as the class is *composed* — the program refuses to compile before a single `Triangle` object exists. And even in an implementation that accepts the class definition, the mistake surfaces at the latest when the method is used: the stub `{ ... }` inherited from the role is real code that dies with `Stub code executed` as soon as anyone calls it.

items: `$shape.^name` asks the object for its class name, so the same `describe` labels

solution.v: each result correctly without knowing the type in advance.

One difference to be aware of: `\w` in Raku is Unicode-aware, so a name such as `café` also passes — which happens to match Raku itself, where `my $café = 1;` is perfectly legal. The spelled-out class `<[A..Za..z0..9_]>` keeps the check strictly ASCII.

Each bracketed group `[ '-' <[A..Za..z]> \w* ]` accepts a hyphen only when a letter follows, so `my-var` is now reported as valid, while `2fast` — and strings like `a-` or `a-1` — still are not.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: `<number>+ % '+'` matches one or more numbers separated by `+` signs — the `%`

solution.v: modifier describes the separator between repetitions.

items: The action method runs when `TOP` matches. `make` attaches a computed value — the

solution.v: sum of the numbers — which `.made` reads back after parsing.

items: A `token` never skips spaces, so this grammar is strict about its input:

solution.v: `'3+4+5'` parses, but `'3 + 4 + 5'` does not (`.parse` returns `Nil`). To accept spaces around the plus signs, make `TOP` a `rule` — and detach the quantifier from its atom:

In a `rule`, whitespace in the pattern stands for an implicit `<.ws>` call. Written as `<number> + % '+'`, with a space before the `+` quantifier, that implied whitespace covers the whole repetition — separators included — so both `'3+4+5'` and `'3 + 4 + 5'` are parsed, and the sum is `12` either way. (If you prefer to stay with a `token`, spell the spaces out in the separator: `<number>+ % [ \s* '+' \s* ]`.)

blocks.v: Small complete programs that lean on several parts of the course at once — data structures, control flow, string handling, and a little maths — the kind of thing you might reach for in real code.

prompt.v: Convert the number `1994` to Roman numerals (the answer is `MCMXCIV`) and print it. Build it up from the standard value–symbol table, largest first.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The table lists every symbol in descending value, including the subtractive

solution.v: forms like `CM` (900) and `IV` (4), so the algorithm never has to special-case them.

items: For each entry, the `while` appends the symbol and subtracts its value as many

solution.v: times as it fits, so the largest pieces are used up first.

prompt.v: Evaluate the reverse-Polish (postfix) expression `3 4 + 5 *`, where each operator acts on the two values before it. The result is `35`. Print it.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Numbers are pushed onto a stack. An operator pops the two most recent values,

solution.v: combines them, and pushes the result back — the essence of postfix evaluation.

items: `do given $token` turns the operator into the right arithmetic, and the order

solution.v: `$a` then `$b` (popped in reverse) keeps subtraction and division the right way round.

prompt.v: Given sales figures `apples => 5, pears => 3, plums => 8`, print a simple bar chart: each label, then a tab, then a bar of `#` characters as long as its value, ordered by label.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: The string repetition operator `x` builds each bar: `'#' x 5` is `#####`. The

solution.v: value simply becomes the bar length.

items: The `\t` between the label and the bar is a tab character, so the bars line up

solution.v: in a column instead of starting right after each name of a different length.

prompt.v: Use the sieve of Eratosthenes to find all prime numbers up to `30` and print them. Start by assuming every number is prime, then cross out the multiples.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Instead of a list of flags, `%composite` remembers which numbers have been

solution.v: crossed out. A number still missing from it when its turn comes is prime.

items: For each prime `$i`, its multiples are generated as the sequence

solution.v: `$i², $i² + $i ... $limit` and marked composite. Starting at `$i²` skips multiples already handled by smaller primes.

items: This is a single [sequence](/paradigms/lazy/sequence-operator), not a C-style

solution.v: `for` header. The `...` operator takes the first two values, works out the step between them, and keeps going up to the limit. For `$i` = `3` that means starting at `9`, then `12`, so the step is `3`, and the loop walks the whole list:
So `for` receives one list to iterate over — `9, 12, 15, …` — rather than three separate clauses.

items: `$i²` squares the number using a Unicode superscript. Raku accepts all three of

solution.v: `$i * $i`, `$i ** 2`, and `$i²` — they compute exactly the same value, so pick whichever reads best to you. The superscript digits (`²`, `³`, …) are ordinary characters you can type or paste directly into the source.

prompt.v: Given the lines `Anna,90`, `Bob,72`, and `Cara,84`, parse each into a name and a score, print the average score, and list everyone who scored above it.

solution.v: Here is a possible solution to the task.

items: Splitting each line on the comma and assigning to `($name, $mark)` unpacks the

solution.v: two fields at once; `.Int` turns the score text into a number.

items: The average is the sum of the values over their count; anyone whose score beats

solution.v: it is listed. Here the average works out to a whole `82`.

items: That final loop can be written as a pipeline. `sort` orders the pairs, `grep`

solution.v: keeps the ones above the average, and `map` reduces each surviving pair to its name — so the loop body carries no logic, only the printing:

Reading left to right, this says exactly what it does: sort, keep the ones above average, take their names. Each stage is a small, self-contained step, and `*.value` / `*.key` are [Whatever stars](/advanced/whatever) that build a one-argument block on the fly.
